articles.title: What is social media monitoring? Full 2026 guide
articles.fullContent:
Key takeaways

  1. Social media monitoring is the practice of tracking brand mentions, keywords, and conversations across social platforms to understand what people are saying about your brand, your competitors, and your industry.
  2. Monitoring helps teams catch reputation risks early, respond to customers faster, and surface insights that inform marketing, product, and sales decisions.
  3. AI-powered monitoring tools can now analyze sentiment, detect crises, and surface trends across millions of sources in real time.
  4. The best monitoring strategies share insights across the organization, not just the social team, and measure ROI tied to business outcomes.

What is social media monitoring?

Social media monitoring is the process of tracking what people are saying about your brand on social media.

This includes both tagged and untagged mentions, whether they show up in comments on your own accounts or in conversations happening elsewhere across the social web.

In practice, that scope is wider than most teams expect. Monitoring covers posts, comments, replies, reviews, video captions, forum threads, and news coverage across networks like Instagram, TikTok, LinkedIn, X, Facebook, YouTube, Reddit, and Bluesky, where 84% of U.S. adults use YouTube and 71% use Facebook. Most of those conversations never tag your handle, which is exactly why manual checking falls short.

Bonus !!!

Take action on customer insights and drive impact for your organization with our complete guide to social listening using Hootsuite x Talkwalker.

Download now

How does social media monitoring work?

Social media monitoring isn’t just one activity. It’s a mix of signals that, together, tell you what people are saying about your brand, your competitors, and your industry.

Here are the key components that make up social media monitoring:

  • Brand mentions: Track when people talk about your brand across comments, posts, and conversations. This is your baseline signal, and it covers both direct tags and untagged references.
  • Sentiment analysis: Understand how people feel about your brand by looking at whether mentions are positive, negative, or neutral. Tracked over time, sentiment tells you whether perception is improving or slipping.
  • Competitor analysis: Keep tabs on what people are saying about your competitors, including their campaigns, products, and gaps. Their weak spots are often your opportunities.
  • Industry trends: Follow larger conversations in your industry, including trending topics, hashtags, and viral moments, so you can join them while they still matter.
  • Influencer identification: Find people already talking about your brand who could become partners or advocates. Existing fans usually convert into partnerships faster than cold outreach.
  • Share of voice (SOV): Measure how much of the conversation your brand owns compared to competitors. It’s one of the clearest ways to benchmark visibility.
  • Crisis detection: Catch spikes in mentions or shifts in sentiment early, so you can respond before things escalate.
  • Hashtag tracking: Monitor how your branded hashtags, campaign tags, and industry keywords are performing.
  • AI-powered analysis: Use AI to cluster themes, flag anomalies, and summarize what thousands of mentions add up to, instead of reading them one by one.

Together, these signals turn everyday social conversations into actionable insights for your team.

Social media monitoring vs. social listening: what’s the difference?

The short answer: monitoring tracks individual conversations as they happen, and social listening analyzes those conversations in aggregate to find patterns. They’re closely related, but they serve different purposes.

  • Social monitoring is reactive. It focuses on tracking mentions and responding to what’s happening in real time.
  • Social listening is proactive. It starts by analyzing the information from social monitoring to spot larger patterns and trends. In other words, it looks at the bigger picture to improve your social media marketing strategy over time.

For example, social media monitoring identifies comments about your brand online that could use an immediate response from your social or customer service teams.

Source: Warby Parker

Social media listening takes a step back and looks at those same comments over time to see how sentiment is changing.

articles.title: Rewatch the Late Dolly Parton’s Iconic Ads Over the Decades
articles.fullContent:
By Christopher Cicchiello The future of brands gets decided here. Join the industry’s top marketers at Brandweek for the ideas, insights, and connections shaping what’s next. Get your ticket.

Dolly Parton, known as the “Queen of Country,” has died at 80 years old, her estate announced on Tuesday (Aug. 25).

Parton wasn’t just the generation-spanning, 11-time Grammy-winning country singer behind hits including “Jolene,” “I Will Always Love You,” and “9 to 5”—the latter of which soundtracked the eponymous film she starred in.

She was also a figure firmly embedded in the fabric of American culture, collaborating with Beyoncé, Post Malone, and Pitbull later in her career.

Always one for the spotlight, Parton brought her talents on the set of numerous commercials over the decades, sporting her iconic platinum blonde bouffant wig.

These are some of the most enduring from Parton’s sprawling career:

Parton has been the face of brands like Breeze Detergent since commercials were in black and white.

Standing beside Porter Wagoner—who introduced the world to a young Parton on his variety show in 1967—the duo showcase bath towels with intricate bouquets of flowers that came in boxes of Breeze detergent.

“Nope, you can only get them in boxes of Breeze,” Wagoner replied.

The same year that Parton released her ABC variety show Dolly and her album Trio alongside Linda Ronstadt and Emmylou Harris, she starred in an ad for Golden Nugget Hotel and Casino in Las Vegas, NV.

Unlike most of her ads, where she plays herself, Parton is an unnamed hotel room attendant in this commercial, alongside real estate developer Stephen Wynn. He tells her that both Frank Sinatra and Kenny Rogers stayed in the room.

“And you know who bit this toast? Dolly Parton!”

Parton squeals in delight: “Dolly Parton is the best!”

It’s a cornball fiesta, but Parton’s commitment to the bit keeps it grounded.

Tennessee Department of Transportation (2006)

Parton’s pride for her Tennessee roots are on full display in this infomercial.

Donning a reflective vest cinched at the waist by a large gold belt, Parton touts recent improvements TDOT made in downtown Knoxville, letting viewers know construction is nearly finished.

“Construction crews will be working faster than my Tennessee tornado can finish up,” Parton said, pronouncing “tornado” as “tardado” with a thick Southern drawl.

Parton couldn’t resist alerting drivers which road detours to take to get to her Dollywood theme park as well.

Parton’s debut on the Super Bowl ad stage saw her flip one her most famous songs on its head, literally.

Teaming up with Squarespace, Parton retooled her track 9 to 5 as 5 to 9. The ad was meant to highlight and celebrate the growing “side hustle” economy, as people were increasingly working on a passion projects outside of the routine hours of 9:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m.

“Working 5 to 9, making something of your own now,” she sings as part of the reworked lyrics.

Parton is once again committing to the bit here, and this time, poking fun at herself.

Shot as a satirical fundraiser video complete with a dreary background, Parton turns to viewers to say America has a major problem.

“So I’m going to get it off my chest,” she said, reaching down her shirt. Parton has always been vocal about her breast implants, but instead of where audience expectations went, she pulled out a phone to declare the issue: 5G phones with limited networks.

Parton’s goddaughter, Miley Cyrus, makes a brief cameo as well, asking how she can support the phones. A sequel to the ad features the two singing an impassioned song titled, Do It for the Phones.

As part of the partnership, T-Mobile donated $250,000 to Cyrus’ Happy Hippie Foundation, which funds programs supporting homeless youth and other vulnerable populations.

Working with Dentsu Creative, the restaurant chain tapped Parton as the face of its “Rewards that Rock” campaign in 2023. At the time, Parton was promoting her album Rockstar. As part of the effort, the chain gave away 667 Parton-branded rocking chairs.

Parton looks every bit the bedazzled rockstar in the commercial.

For one day only in 2024, Krispy Kreme encouraged everyone to harness their inner Parton.

Big brands can be expected to mismanage a product launch or a campaign now and again, but the past two weeks have produced three especially egregious examples of marketing tone deafness—and that’s being generous.

Neutrogena responded to Hayden Panettiere’s allegations against the brand four days after her death. Target hastily pulled an offensive Halloween costume off shelves. And Good Good Golf has taken down a video that casually depicted violence toward women.

All of the brands have issued mea culpas. (None responded to ADWEEK’s request for comment.) But the incidents leave troubling questions. In the wake of past explosive brand gaffes—Pepsi’s Kendall Jenner spot comes to mind—why do big, sophisticated companies keep offending their own customers?

Mike Kresch, vp of strategy for digital marketing agency Moburst, said that brands have a duty to examine their products and marketing closely before releasing them.

articles.title: Social media SWOT analysis: A 2026 guide with template
articles.fullContent:
Key takeaways

  1. A social media SWOT analysis evaluates your performance across four areas: strengths, weaknesses, opportunities, and threats, so you can make strategic decisions grounded in data.
  2. Run one when you’re planning budgets, launching campaigns, conducting your annual audit, or responding to a sudden shift in sentiment.
  3. The most useful analyses combine internal performance data with external signals like competitor activity, industry benchmarks, and platform changes.
  4. This guide includes step-by-step instructions, concrete examples for each quadrant, and a ready-to-use template.

What is a social media SWOT analysis?

A social media SWOT analysis is a framework marketers use to evaluate their social media performance by looking at four areas: strengths, weaknesses, opportunities, and threats.

Here are a few scenarios where a social media SWOT analysis could come in handy:

  • Deciding whether to join a new social media platform
  • Rebranding or repositioning
  • Making budget decisions
  • Planning campaigns
  • Identifying emerging trends

In short, a social media SWOT analysis helps you make smarter decisions about where and how to invest on social. It also keeps your strategy grounded in real data, not guesswork.

What are the components of a social media SWOT analysis?

There are four components, and each one maps to a different type of insight:

  • Strengths: What your brand is doing well on social media, like strong engagement, high follower count, or consistent branding. Example: your Instagram Reels consistently outperform your static posts, or your community responds fast to every product drop.
  • Weaknesses: Areas where your brand could improve, from inconsistent posting to off-target messaging. Example: no presence on an emerging platform your audience already uses, or slow response times in your inbox.
  • Opportunities: External factors that give your brand a chance to grow, like emerging trends or new platform features. Example: a rising keyword in your category, or a new video format with an early-adopter boost.
  • Threats: External risks that could hurt your performance, like algorithm changes or increased competition. Example: a rival brand launching on a channel you’ve deprioritized.

Strengths and weaknesses look at internal factors you can control, while opportunities and threats focus on external factors. These things happen outside of your control (but you still need to monitor and respond to them).

How is a social media SWOT different from a traditional SWOT?

A social media SWOT pulls from different data than a traditional business SWOT. Instead of market share, revenue, and supply chain factors, you’re working with platform metrics, social listening signals, and competitive benchmarks that update daily.

Speed is the other difference. Social platforms shift faster than most business environments, so a social media SWOT needs revisiting quarterly rather than once a year.

Why run a social media SWOT analysis?

A social media SWOT analysis helps you see the bigger picture, so you can see what’s working, what’s not, and decide what to do next.

Here’s why you should conduct a social media SWOT analysis:

Set impactful (but realistic) goals

For goals to be effective, they need to be ambitious but achievable. A social media SWOT analysis helps you understand what’s actually possible by combining your past performance with industry benchmarks.

In other words, a SWOT analysis grounds your goal-setting in both internal data and external reality. That’s how you set business goals that actually hold up.

Identify and mitigate risks

Weaknesses and threats might sound scary. But taking a good, hard look at these areas will help you prepare for potential curveballs.

Weaknesses reveal internal risks related to process, tools, and teams. Threats point to external challenges like algorithm shifts, compliance issues, or economic changes.

articles.title: Fans Have More Friends: Heineken’s Formula for Real-Life Connection
articles.fullContent:
By Matt Britton The future of brands gets decided here. Join the industry’s top marketers at Brandweek for the ideas, insights, and connections shaping what’s next. Get your ticket.

Culture moves quickly, but brands that chase every new behavior, platform or conversation, with that same speed, risk losing their way. For marketers, the harder challenge is knowing which changes genuinely belong within the brand and which ones are better left alone.

This episode of The Speed of Culture podcast features Alison Payne, chief marketing officer at Heineken USA, joining host Matt Britton to examine how Heineken responds to changing consumer behavior while holding onto its core: The brand exists to make social moments better.

Their conversation explores what that principle means for experiential marketing, fandom, AI, moderation, packaging, and the creative decisions marketers have to protect inside complex organizations.

Alison Payne is the chief marketing officer at Heineken USA, where she leads marketing across a portfolio that includes Heineken and Dos Equis. Across her career, she has helped grow major consumer brands spanning beer, spirits, food and wellness, including Guinness, Smirnoff, Lay’s, Doritos and Special K.

Her experience across categories has shaped an approach to marketing grounded in brand positioning, consumer behavior, creative excellence, and disciplined execution. At Heineken, her work includes major cultural platforms such as the US Open, Formula 1, gaming, creator partnerships, and the continued expansion of the non-alcoholic beer category.

[00:38] Stay Relevant Without Losing the Brand — Alison argues that responding to culture does not mean following every trend. A more useful filter to apply is whether a new behavior, platform, or conversation fits what the brand already stands for. For Heineken, that means evolving the places and occasions where socializing happens while protecting the underlying idea of bringing people together over good times.

[05:20] From Badge Sponsorships to Consumer Journeys — Experiential marketing no longer begins when someone enters an event and ends when they leave. Alison describes how Heineken approaches properties such as Coachella and the US Open across the entire before, during and after experience. The anticipation, live moment, social conversation, collectibles and memories all become part of the platform, giving marketers far more to work with than traditional logo placement.

[10:59] Why Fandom Creates Social Connection — Heineken’s “Fans Have More Friends” platform is built on an insight that fandom gives people an immediate reason to connect. Alison explains how shared passions can turn strangers into friends, whether they are supporting Arsenal at a bar or following their country during a tournament. For brands, the opportunity lies less in inserting themselves into fandom, and more in helping fans experience that connection together.

[15:08] Using AI to Get to Better Ideas, Faster — Heineken is experimenting with AI, but Alison draws a clear line between acceleration and authenticity. The technology can help teams simulate creative ideas, test them quickly with consumers, summarize information and remove administrative work. But for a brand built around real social experiences, manufacturing fake human moments would work against the very thing the brand represents.

[21:32] Moderation as a New Social Behavior — The growth of non-alcoholic beer reflects a broader change in how consumers approach drinking occasions. Alison describes behaviors such as “zebra striping,” where people alternate between alcoholic and non-alcoholic options, and “social marathoning,” where they want to remain part of a long social occasion while staying in control. Heineken 0.0 gives consumers a way to change what they are drinking without stepping outside the social moment.

[30:01] Strategy Often Lies in Saying ‘No’ — One of Alison’s earliest marketing lessons was that strategy is defined as much by what a brand refuses to do as what it chooses to pursue. That discipline becomes increasingly important as marketers face endless opportunities, cultural conversations, and internal pet projects. She also stresses the need to kill weak ideas early while protecting strong creative work from being diluted through layers of organizational consensus.

articles.title: Ad-Supported Streaming Keeps Growing While Broadcast Falls
articles.fullContent:
By Mark Mwachiro Streaming viewers are getting more comfortable with ads. That is one of the key takeaways from Nielsen’s Q2 2026 Ad-Supported Gauge released on Tuesday.

Ad-supported streaming grew +1.6% in the second quarter to 48.2%, continuing to eat into linear segments.

Together, broadcast and cable ad-supported viewing represented 51.8%. Cable held steady at 25.2%, while the broadcast segment, despite the presence of the NBA Finals and the early stages of the World Cup, fell from 28.2% to 26.6%.

These two major tournaments were also available on streaming, which may have led to internal audience cannibalization, as the NBA Finals, which aired on ABC, was also available to stream on the ESPN app, both of which are owned by Disney.

Meanwhile, the World Cup’s English media rights aired on the linear channels Fox and FS1 and streamed on Fox One. Telemundo held the Spanish media rights for the tournament, airing on the linear channel and streaming on Peacock.

Streaming enables mobile viewing, allowing audiences to catch up on games on the go. This frees them from static screens, which may have contributed to the broadcast segment’s decline despite the availability of those premium products.

However, it was not all bad news for the broadcast segment, as it rose +0.6% year-over-year to 26.6% from 26% compared to the second quarter of 2025.

Overall, ad-supported TV finished the quarter with a 71.5% share of total viewing, down -1.3% from its performance in the first quarter. Non-ad-supported TV ended Q2 with a 28.5% share.

articles.title: How to manage social media as a one-person team
articles.fullContent:
As the hub of cultural conversations and online activity, social media provides valuable intelligence to inform business strategies. It’s how you discover everything from what trends are taking over to what products people are buying. In fact, the 2026 Social Intelligence Report found that half of one-person teams consider it mission-critical for future growth.

But between crafting content and staying on top of communications, managing social media is hard enough when you’re the only one on the team. This leaves you with little time to focus on social intelligence, let alone extract insights to fuel business growth.

In this post, we provide a guideline on how to streamline social media management for one-person teams. From strategic automation to structured task management, we show you how you can save time and focus on more high-impact work. Let’s get started.

What it means to run social alone

When you’re running social media on your own, you’re juggling multiple roles. You’re the one coming up with content ideas and bringing those ideas to fruition by writing captions and designing graphics. At the same time, you’re in charge of publishing the content, managing comments, responding to DMs and analyzing your data.

You’re essentially doing everything by yourself all at once.

As it is, social media marketers are already at risk of burning out and running out of content ideas. The 2025 Sprout Social Index TM notes that 33% of marketers fear burnout and creative fatigue.

The risk gets significantly bigger for someone who’s constantly overwhelmed because they’re doing it all alone. Yet this is what social media management looks like for most startups and small business operations.

The biggest challenges for a one-person team

To start with, you need to pinpoint what actually makes it challenging to manage social media on your own. That way, you can focus your efforts on tackling those specific challenges. Let’s dig deeper into the biggest problems in social media management for one-person teams.

Constant context-switching across platforms

One minute you’re checking your Facebook stats, the next you’re trying to catch up on all your Instagram DMs and messages. When you’re a one-person social media team, you’re constantly switching between different tasks across platforms. So you’re distracted and unable to focus on a single task, which will affect productivity.

It’s even worse when you’re doing everything manually. According to The Social Media Productivity Report, 63% of social media marketers report not being able to do high-impact work because of manual tasks.

Creative and content fatigue

Social media teams have to always be on top of trending memes and viral topics to keep producing relevant content. According to the 2025 Sprout Social Index TM , 94% of social media practitioners report having to be chronically online to do their jobs.

Ultimately, the social media burnout catches up, especially when you’re the only one coming up with ideas and producing content. That’s why burnout and creative fatigue rank as the fourth greatest fear among social media marketers.

Proving ROI without a dedicated analyst

When you’re the only one on your team, you’re also in charge of collecting performance data and putting together reports. It’s easy enough to point out which content is performing well or how your page has grown over time. But without a dedicated analyst to interpret your data, you’ll have a hard time aligning your social media investment to actual business outcomes.

Keeping up with response-time expectations

Between the content creation and performance analysis, comments and DMs often go unanswered for hours when you’re a one-person team. This could reflect poorly on the customer experience, especially with consumers expecting swift responses on social media.

As the 2025 Sprout Social Index TM found, almost three-quarters of consumers expect brands to respond within 24 hours. They’ll even buy from a competitor next time if the brand doesn’t respond to their customer service questions on social.

3 tips for prioritizing when everything feels urgent

You’re a few days behind on content and your DMs are flooded with messages that you haven’t been able to check. For one-person social teams, it seems like there’s a never-ending to-do list where every item needs to be done “right now.” Here’s how you can streamline your tasks and figure out what to prioritize:

1. Set 2–3 goals tied to business outcomes, not vanity metrics

Impressions are great, but what do they actually mean for your business? Have a clear idea of what you want to get out of social media. This will serve as the foundation for the rest of your social media marketing strategy, shaping everything from your content to your analytics.

Start with 2-3 goals that are related to actual business outcomes. For instance:

  • Growing brand awareness
  • Building a brand community
  • Improving brand sentiment
  • Generating online sales
  • Driving qualified leads
  • Preventing customer churn
  • Speeding up social customer service

2. Use an impact-vs-effort framework to triage daily tasks

Building a framework for prioritizing tasks will help you organize your schedule more strategically. Weigh the expected value of each task against the effort needed to complete it, so you can sort out the order in which to do them.

For example:

Quick wins (high impact, low effort)

  • What they are: Tasks that yield high value and require very little time or money
  • Examples: Repurposing existing content into graphics and bite-sized social posts, sharing user-generated content, customizing social media templates for new ideas, actively replying to recent comments

Big bets (high impact, high effort)

  • What they are: Tasks that yield high value and require heavy planning, time and/or budget
  • Examples: Running an influencer marketing campaign, launching a multi-platform content series

Backups (low impact, low effort)

  • What they are: Minor tasks that don’t add significant value but take very little time to complete
  • Examples: Making small tweaks to your profile, engaging with content from other brands/creators

Time sinkers (low impact, high effort)

  • What they are: Time-consuming tasks that yield little to no return on investment
  • Examples: Manually tracking and analyzing vanity metrics, designing complex custom graphics for platforms that your audience doesn’t use

3. Pick one or two networks instead of trying to be everywhere

articles.title: Reports Indicate Google’s Spam Update Focused On SEO AI Content via @sejournal, @martinibuster
articles.fullContent:
Reports online suggest that at least a part of Google’s August Spam Update was about removing AI-generated SEO content that was expressly created for ranking for search engines. Google recently published a research paper about catching this kind of spam, so that’s another clue.

Google’s Scalable Cluster Termination System

It’s well-known that just because content was created with AI does not make it spammy. Maybe less understood is that any content that’s created in a way that’s meant to rank for keywords tends to go up to the line between normal content and spam, if not actually cross over that line.

Reports online seem to indicate that Google has implemented something new to catch AI-generated content that crosses that line. Something that’s not well known is that Google recently published a research paper called Scalable Cluster Termination System (S-CTS) that is designed to “terminate” networks of mass-generated AI spam.

That doesn’t mean that Google’s August Spam Update was all about AI generated content. But if the reports are correct, this kind of AI content may be the reason why many sites lost rankings.

“Regarding this Google spam update, it seems that sites automatically posting with Claude Code, codec, etc., are being filtered and dropped across the board.

It’s possible they’re automatically detecting it by attaching some kind of AI credit, similar to generated images or videos.

However, sites that initially had a vibe of manually posting bit by bit—like the attached image—and then switched to LLM automation afterward appear to be surviving in some cases.

Sites created entirely with full automation from the start have zero “trust signals” from Google, whereas sites that were manually operated early on have accumulated domain trust (trust savings) and past engagement data.

As a result, even if they switch to LLM automated posting later, the existing domain evaluation acts as a buffer, making it harder for them to immediately receive spam judgments (or automatic penalties)…

The sample size is small, so this is by no means definitive—just a trend—but in this day and age when you don’t even need to open the WordPress editor screen anymore, there’s a good chance they’re using AI credits for text too to determine manual penalties or automatic penalties, right?”

Users Trust Websites. It’s Not A Trust Signal. It’s a User Signal.

Google doesn’t use “trust signals” exactly but Google does use user generated signals that can show that a site is trusted by users. I think it’s helpful to make the distinction between user generated signals and an abstract “trust signal” which doesn’t tell you anything about what it is.

That same person followed up with another tweet saying that a Japanese journal that publishes AI-generated content has not been caught in the recent spam update but they also noted that all content is hand-checked by humans before publishing.

“…but so far it hasn’t received any penalties (naturally, we do manual visual checks by humans before publishing articles).

In the initial stage, leveraging SNS and press releases to spread awareness, improve crawlability, and attract impressions might be what’s working.”

Of course, not everyone agreed with that post because it’s anecdotal.

@seiichi_satoweb suggested that it’s not that the content was AI-generated that may be problematic but rather that AI was used to generate content that manipulates the search results.

“Companies operating media should check the rankings from August 18 to 21.

…If it dropped, I think the first thing to suspect is not the quality of the articles, but the “method of mass production.”

Google defines the malicious use of mass-generated content as generating a large number of pages primarily for manipulating search rankings, not for supporting users.

It’s not about whether it was created with generative AI, but what it was created for that they’re looking at.

Companies that are increasing their volume with AI should definitely check this once.”

Even over on the Blackhat World Forums the members there were complaining about how frustrating it is to encounter AI slop that’s taking over the search results.

“They’ve finally realized that AI slop is taking over.

I did a search recently for a quick tutorial on how to change settings in an app and saw 4 back to back sites clearly spun up with AI to create articles answering that – all looked exactly the same, same AI slop formatting of subheadings and bullets, poor spacing between the sections, 3 sentences basically expanded into a 500 words.

AI slop pages is the new doorway page and Google is struggling to reel it in.”

Another member responded that they tend to add unique qualities to their AI-generated content so that it’s not a pure template-driven content.

Of course, there were others who remarked that their AI-generated content improved after the update, as noted in the private Google SEO Mastermind Facebook group .

Nevertheless, a rule of thumb that everyone should follow, regardless of how the content was created, is that content that is strongly focused on keywords have been hurting for the past couple years. Auto-generating content to capitalize on SEO trends might have been one of the targets of the recent spam update.

By Adweek Staff The future of brands gets decided here. Join the industry’s top marketers at Brandweek for the ideas, insights, and connections shaping what’s next. Get your ticket.

What if purpose and performance weren’t mutually exclusive while building a brand?

In this episode of Adspeak by ADWEEK, host Audrey Kemp brings together R. Ethan Braden, VP and CMCO at Texas A&M University, and Tyler Merrick, founder and CEO of Joyride, to explore how very different brands can turn authentic storytelling and bold marketing decisions into measurable growth.

Ethan shares how Texas A&M modernized a 150-year-old brand without losing its core values, including the campaign that generated 80 million YouTube views.

Tyler reveals how Joyride used product differentiation, cultural relevance, and genuine creator partnerships to become the No. 1 candy at Target.

Together, they unpack why purpose-driven marketing works best when it is grounded in authentic brand positioning, strong creative conviction, and a clear understanding of the audience.

From legacy institutions to challenger brands, this conversation offers practical lessons for building brands that matter and perform.

How to reposition a legacy brand nationally by what makes you distinct

Why pulling underperforming creative can catalyze breakthrough results

The three-legged stool framework for challenger brand success

How to validate purpose-driven positioning through retail performance

The difference between hiring an influencer and building a partnership

How to maintain brand integrity while modernizing for national relevance

R. Ethan Braden is VP and chief marketing and communications officer at Texas A&M University, where he leads brand, marketing, communications, and storytelling to strengthen the university’s national presence. Previously, he served as EVP and CMO at Purdue University and Purdue Global. Earlier, Ethan spent more than a decade at Eli Lilly & Company, helping lead billion-dollar brands including Cymbalta and Jardiance. In 2023, he was named Content Marketer of the Year by the Content Marketing Institute.

Tyler Merrick is the founder and CEO of Joyride, a challenger candy brand that became the #1-selling candy at Target by combining clean ingredients with authentic creator partnerships. With roots in family entrepreneurship and a background in product development across multiple categories, Merrick built Joyride on a thesis of purpose-driven performance: delivering significantly less sugar and zero artificial additives without compromising taste.

[04:43] Export Your Brand’s Distinctiveness Beyond Insider Culture — Ethan explains why Texas A&M had to move beyond insider mythology to build national relevance. Research showed outsiders primarily associated the university with football, sports, Aggies, and agriculture. By repositioning around “best university in the world,” Texas A&M translated its distinctive culture into a message outsiders could understand, generating 80 million YouTube views, with 88% coming from beyond Texas.

[08:57] Three Forces Behind Joyride’s Challenger Brand Breakthrough — Tyler breaks down Joyride’s growth through three forces working together: a differentiated product, cultural relevance, and an authentic creator partnership. Lower sugar and clean ingredients met a generation looking for a new candy brand, while Ryan Trahan brought genuine credibility. The lesson is simple: product-market fit, cultural timing, and the right creator can turn challenger brands into cultural forces today.

[12:57] Use Core Values to Modernize Without Losing Your Identity — Ethan explains how Texas A&M uses its RELLIS values: Respect, Excellence, Leadership, Loyalty, Integrity, and Selfless Service, as guardrails for modernization. Rather than asking whether an idea is traditionally “on brand,” the team asks whether it is “in character.” This framework helps leaders make bold creative choices while reassuring legacy stakeholders that evolution can strengthen, rather than compromise, institutional identity over time.

[14:53] Why Authentic, DIY Content Can Beat Big-Budget Production — Tyler reveals why Joyride deliberately favors grassroots-looking content over highly polished production. With 2.1 million engaged Instagram followers, the brand has built trust through self-shot, transparent content that feels more like a community than advertising. By showing failures, improvements, and authentic moments, Joyride makes audiences feel included. For challenger brands, relatability and frequency can outperform expensive production at scale.

[17:02] Pull Failing Creative to Make Room for Breakthrough Ideas — Ethan shares the bold decision to pull an underperforming Texas A&M ad rather than continue optimizing a campaign that was not working. The team went dark before launching a values-driven commercial during the Texas A&M–Notre Dame game. With a target of one million YouTube views, the campaign reached 6.5 million in weeks, proving decisive creative action can unlock breakthrough performance.

[20:56] Test Purpose-Driven Positioning Across Diverse Retail Channels — Tyler explains how Joyride tested its clean-ingredient positioning beyond traditional better-for-you retail. Exclusive flavors at 7-Eleven and HEB performed strongly across channels, even attracting parents who had not visited 7-Eleven in years. The strategy showed that purpose-driven positioning can travel when brands adapt products to each channel’s culture, creating experiences that feel relevant rather than simply expanding distribution confidently now.

articles.fullContent:
By Mark Stenberg The sports news brand Front Office Sports will launch its first mobile app Sept. 1, the first of two major product launches from the publisher in recent weeks.

The release precedes the Sept. 14 debut of Front Office Sports Tonight, a nationally syndicated daily television show, where the digitally native publisher expands into linear programming for the first time.

The mobile app, designed in-house but built in partnership with the developer Pug Pig, aims to deepen engagement by offering its most loyal audiences a dedicated home for Front Office Sports content and its slew of new programming.

“We have grown from being a newsletter business into a website, social channels, YouTube, and, beginning this month, linear television,” said vice president of marketing and strategy Victoria Baldwin Dailey. “Eighty-one percent of our audience say that engaging with FOS is a daily habit, so we knew that if we created an app, people would come to it.”

The app’s robust data signals could, in future, better inform editorial decisions, said Baldwin Dailey.

In October 2024, the sports news brand sold a majority ownership stake to RedBird IMI, a joint investment fund led by former CNN executive Jeff Zucker. Financial details of the deal were not disclosed.

This year, Front Office Sports is pacing to surpass $20 million in revenue and achieve profitability, according to chief executive and founder Adam White.

The company, which is almost entirely ad-funded, will introduce additional advertising inventory and exclusive sponsorship opportunities in the app, including The Pole Position, an exclusive takeover of its landing page.

The new offerings also reflect a growing trend, as publishers embrace video and launch apps in response to declining web traffic, a result of disruption posed by artificial intelligence.

Over the last two years, The New York Times added a vertical video Watch tab to its app, People Magazine introduced an app-exclusive reality show , and Eater belatedly launched a mobile platform of its own.

Front Office Sports is less affected by traffic fluctuations than its peers given its origins as a newsletter publisher, according to White, but the app gives it a more direct line into its audiences.

In total, the app will have five separate tabs: Now, Read, Watch, Play, and For You.

Together, the sections will make available all the content that lives on the website, in addition to multimedia programming and some exclusive elements.

The Now tab will serve as the landing page. Modeled on the flagship newsletter, the section will feature an array of content, including a full-bleed centerpiece story, two recent stories underneath, audio from the latest episode of its flagship podcast Front Office Sports Today, a push to play its daily Factle Sports trivia game, and a carousel of recent vertical video.

The Read tab will feature its latest written reporting. While the Watch section will feature video from its flagship podcast, long-form YouTube series, short-form vertical video, and, starting this fall, clips from Front Office Sports Tonight.

FOR Scoops, Sharp Analysis, and Insider Context

On Background A direct line to ADWEEK’S senior media reporter, delivering scoops, sharp analysis, and insider context on how publishing, streaming, and advertising are changing.

By submitting your email, you agree to our Terms of Use and Privacy Policy . You may opt-out anytime by clicking ‘unsubscribe’ from the newsletter or from your account.

“The short-form video component is particularly interesting because we’re increasingly seeing the Reels or TikTok-style experience become a standard part of media products themselves,” said FTI Consulting senior managing director Justin Eisenband. “Sports is especially well suited to this type of experience because so much of the value is tied to specific moments.”

The fourth tab, Play, is a big point of emphasis for the editorial brand, according to Baldwin Dailey.

Front Office Sports currently has two games on offer, Factle and Factle Sports trivia, which will be available to play in-app via webview.

Finally, the fifth tab, For You, will let people customize their app experience, like by following specific authors and topics.

Newsletters will not be available to read in the mobile app, as the publisher wanted to respect users’ preference to read emails in their inbox, but people can sign up from the app.

In addition to its enhanced video footprint, the publisher is running events, like the annual Huddle in the Hamptons event it hosts in July.

This expansion, although driven by necessity, is vital, according to Eisenband.

Key Takeaways

  • Franchise costs range widely. A home-based franchise starts at around $10,000, while a McDonald’s franchise ranges from $1.47 million to $2.73 million per its 2026 FDD. 
  • Every franchisor must provide a Franchise Disclosure Document (FDD). Use it to compare key factors such as fee structures and available support and financing across brands. 
  • Marketing is critical from day one. Brand awareness gets customers searching, but the franchise location with the strongest local marketing presence wins. 
  • Local SEO and geo-targeted paid ads are the two highest-ROI channels for new franchisees, closely followed by social media that stays within brand guidelines. 
  • Franchise earnings vary widely. Franchisees in the food and beverage space can earn anywhere from under $50,000 to over $250,000.

Learning how to start a franchise can be a great way to become a business owner. To launch a business, you need to perform market research, file for a license, create a marketing plan, and build your brand. Buying a franchise location within a corporation that’s already taken all those steps is one way to shorten that learning curve.

Becoming a franchise business owner also enables you to tap into a large brand’s resources and branding, but that doesn’t mean you should leave the marketing completely up to them.

Savvy entrepreneurs who start a franchise business understand the importance of taking all the right steps from start to finish. That’s exactly what I’m here to show you in this guide.

We’ll cover the basics, like how to start a franchise and the initial costs. Then we’ll move on to the engine that makes your franchise a success: learning how to market it once it’s open.

How Does a Franchise Business Work?

In a franchise business, a franchise owner pays a fee to essentially “rent” a brand name. The franchisee runs the business themselves (or hires someone to do so) and must follow the rules and regulations governing brand use.

For example, many McDonald’s restaurants are franchises, meaning an owner (or group of owners, in some cases) pays McDonald’s to use their brand name, menus, logos, and other business assets.

They run their location, pay McDonald’s to use the name, and keep the remaining profits.

A franchise business is a popular business model because it offers owners the best of both worlds: the support of a large brand and the benefits of owning a business.

A few businesses that offer franchising options include:

  • 7-Eleven
  • Taco Bell
  • Great Clips
  • Ace Hardware

Starting a franchise business should not be taken lightly. There are pros and cons to consider before deciding whether to become a franchisee.

Benefits of Starting a Franchise Business

Starting a business gives you more control over your life and income. Unlike starting your own business, however, buying into a franchise offers specific benefits.

More Support

Starting a franchise business is sort of like playing video games on easy mode. The franchisor offers support through training, materials, process flows, and branding to help you get your business off the ground.

For example, starting a taco shop could require months of menu development, taste testing, logo design, and product sourcing. As a Taco Bell franchise owner, however, much of that work is already completed.

Lower Failure Rate

Franchise businesses may offer you a better chance of success than going it alone. When you buy into a franchise, you join a proven business model that works. You also have additional support and business resources that can make a difference in your success.

Built-In Brand Awareness

Building a brand is one of the best things you can do for your business. However, it often takes time and resources.

When you buy into a franchise, the branding is already complete. People already know who your brand is and what it represents. This saves you time and creates a built-in customer base you can tap into.

Better Buying Power

In some cases, you may purchase goods at a lower rate. Many franchisors negotiate contracts with vendors for the entire network, allowing you to spend less on goods and services by purchasing in bulk. However, the flip side of these benefits is that you may not be able to choose your vendors, and costs may be higher.

Drawbacks of Owning a Franchise

While there are many benefits to starting a franchise business, there are some drawbacks to keep in mind. You’ll pay licensing fees to corporations, which can eat into profits. You’ll also have less control over some aspects of your business. For example, if you own a franchise restaurant, you may have little to say on the menu or which vendors you use.

How to Start a Franchise Business: 7 Steps

Now that you understand the pros and cons, the next question is: how do you start a franchise business?  This seven-step plan will walk you through everything you need to know.

1. Identify a Business Opportunity

The first step in starting a franchise business is choosing a franchise to invest in. Hundreds of companies offer franchise opportunities: which one is right for you?

articles.title: Paid Media Forecasting: How to Predict Ad Performance (Without Getting It Wrong)

Key Takeaways

  • Paid media forecasts most often break at CPC inflation and conversion rate volatility, not at the strategy level.
  • New campaigns run negative for the first several weeks as algorithms learn. Forecasts that skip this ramp-up period set expectations that fail before the campaign does.
  • Creative decay is a predictable variable that belongs in every paid forecast from day one.
  • AI bidding on Google and Meta is reducing predictability. Bid strategy adjustments have less direct impact than most teams assume.
  • The paid forecasting framework runs in sequence: forecast reach, then efficiency, then profitability. Each step feeds the next.

Your forecast said this campaign would hit a 4x ROAS by month two. Instead, CPCs are up, CTR is sliding, and leadership is asking questions you don’t have good answers to.

This isn’t a strategy problem. It’s a forecasting problem.

Most paid media forecasts fail not because marketers are bad at math, but because they rely on assumptions that don’t survive contact with real auction behavior. CPC inflation, conversion rate volatility, creative decay, and AI bidding unpredictability all create gaps between what the model projected and what the campaign actually delivered.

This post covers what causes those gaps and how to build paid media forecasting models that account for real-world variables from the start, so your next forecast holds up.

Why Paid Media Forecasts Miss

Most paid forecasts break at the same pressure points. Identifying which variable caused a miss is as important as building the next forecast, because the same failure tends to repeat if you don’t isolate the cause.

Source

CPC inflation. CPCs are driven by auction dynamics, not advertiser intention. Competitive pressure, quality score changes, and platform algorithm updates can push CPCs above forecast assumptions faster than most models account for. NP Digital data from campaigns across industries shows CPC inflation leads paid forecast failures at 54 percent, making it the single most common cause of forecast drift.

Conversion rate volatility. Conversion rates don’t hold steady across changing conditions. They compress when buyer confidence drops and expand during periods of strong demand, regardless of traffic quality. A constant conversion rate assumption during an economic downturn is actually a win. A constant assumption during a category boom is a miss waiting to happen. Volatility in conversion rates is always relative to what’s happening outside the platform.

Creative decay. As creative fatigue sets in across any audience, CTR drops and effective CPCs rise. If the forecast doesn’t account for a creative refresh cadence, the model drifts optimistic over the life of the campaign. Creative decay is not an edge case. It is a predictable curve.

AI bidding unpredictability. Automated bidding systems on Google Ads and Meta optimize toward signals the advertiser does not fully control. Teams often assume they can compensate for a weak period by adjusting bids. In practice, bid strategy changes have less direct impact than most assume, because the algorithm is making more of the decisions.

Audience overlap across platforms. When the same audience is targeted across multiple channels simultaneously, reach projections overstate real incremental reach and efficiency metrics overstate actual performance. A lead attributed to paid search and a lead attributed to paid social may be the same person, and the forecast rarely accounts for that.

The Ramp-Up Curve: Why New Campaigns Run Negative First

Forecasting average performance from day one is one of the most reliable ways to lose leadership trust in a new campaign. New paid campaigns almost always run negative through the first several weeks, and a forecast that doesn’t show this sets expectations the campaign will fail to meet before it finds its footing.

The reason is structural. New campaigns require time for bid algorithms to gather enough conversion signals to optimize effectively, for audience targeting to sharpen based on early engagement data, and for creative performance data to inform delivery decisions. During this learning phase, CPCs are typically higher than steady state and conversion rates are lower. That combination produces a negative return that looks like failure but is actually normal.

This effect is most pronounced in Performance Max and Advantage+ campaigns, where the algorithm has broader targeting latitude and less historical data to draw on at launch. Campaigns built on new creative, new landing pages, or new audiences extend the ramp-up period further.

The practical implication for ad forecasting is to model week-by-week profitability, not campaign-average profitability. A campaign that looks marginally profitable in aggregate may be deeply negative in weeks one through three and significantly profitable from week six onward. A flat average across the campaign period hides the early risk and the later opportunity, and gives leadership no framework for interpreting early results.

Teams that show leadership the ramp-up curve before it happens get the time to let campaigns mature. Teams that don’t tend to get pulled before the algorithm has learned anything useful.

The Three-Step Paid Forecasting Framework

A reliable forecast marketing campaign model answers questions in sequence: how many people will see your ads, how many will act on them, and what will the business get in return. Key takeaways

  1. The 10 types of social media interactions are comments, shares, saves, direct messages, tags and mentions, likes and reactions, follows and unfollows, reviews and ratings, social search actions, and interactive content like polls and quizzes.
  2. Not all interactions carry equal weight. Comments, shares, saves, and DMs signal stronger intent than likes alone and have a bigger impact on reach and conversions.
  3. Measuring interaction quality, not just volume, helps teams prove social’s business impact and refine their strategy.
  4. A connected social operating system like Hootsuite Social OS helps teams track, respond to, and learn from interactions across every platform in one place.

What is social media interaction?

Social media interaction is any exchange between a brand and a user on a social platform. That includes likes, comments, direct messages, tags, saves, shares, reviews, and follows.

Interactions happen everywhere 5.75 billion people spend time on social, not just in the feed. They show up in stories, in comment threads, in the DM inbox, and increasingly in search results inside apps like TikTok and Instagram.

The key thing to remember is that interaction is two-way communication. A user can start it, or your brand can. Both directions count, and both shape how people see you.

What is the difference between social media interaction and engagement?

A social media interaction is a single action someone takes, while engagement is the broader measure of how actively your audience interacts with your content over time. In other words, interactions are the individual moments, and engagement is the pattern those moments create.

Why are social media interactions important?

Social media interactions are how people connect with your brand, and vice versa. Every interaction is a chance to build a relationship, answer a question, or move someone closer to a purchase.

There are three reasons interactions deserve attention beyond the vanity metric:

  • They build brand loyalty and trust: Replying to a comment or resolving a DM turns a passive follower into someone with a reason to come back.
  • They influence social search and discovery: Comments, saves, and shares feed the ranking signals platforms use to surface content in feeds and in-app search results.
  • They support customer service and community: A growing share of support questions now arrive as comments and DMs rather than emails or phone calls.

Square’s research on the future of commerce found that interacting with brands is a key part of the buying journey. For example, 46% of consumers want to communicate with businesses through social media platforms.

Summary: Social media interactions open the door to deeper engagement, stronger relationships, and ultimately, conversions.

How consumers expect to interact with brands in 2026

Expectations have shifted in three ways worth planning around.

First, private channels are doing more work. Social users spend more time in DMs, and more sales and support conversations now start in the inbox, which makes the DM thread a customer service channel, not just a marketing one.

Second, people expect speed. A question left sitting for days reads as a non-answer, and it is often visible to everyone else scrolling your comments.

Third, people want interactions that sound human. A reply written like a press release lands worse than a short, direct one.

10 types of social media interactions and how to respond

Here are the 10 most common types of social media interactions, roughly ordered from highest to lowest intent:

  1. Comments and conversations
  2. Shares
  3. Saves
  4. Direct messages
  5. Tags and mentions
  6. Likes and reactions
  7. Follows and unfollows
  8. Reviews and ratings
  9. Social search clicks and actions
  10. Polls, quizzes, and interactive content

1. Comments and conversations

Comments are when users reply directly to your posts, whether that’s with text, emojis, or by tagging other accounts. They’re also the interaction most likely to turn into a real conversation.

Think of comments as soft leads. Someone stopped scrolling, paid attention to your content, and took the time to respond. That’s intent.

Comment threads also carry weight in algorithm prioritization. When a post keeps generating replies, platforms read that as a signal the content is worth showing to more people. Your own replies count toward that activity.

But if you’re ghosting your own comment section, you’re missing out on opportunities to move potential customers closer to decision. That’s why responding back matters.

A social listening strategy is a plan for using social listening to gather information that can help your business succeed. It defines what you track, why you track it, how often you review it, and who sees the results.

Like any good strategy, a social media listening strategy starts with clear goals. From there, it’s all about planning how to gather the right data to support those goals.

You’ll also need to include a plan for analyzing your data and sharing your results and strategic recommendations.

In practice, a complete social listening strategy usually covers five components:

  • Goals: The business outcomes your listening supports, from reputation management to product research.
  • Keywords and channels: The brands, products, competitors, topics, and platforms you monitor.
  • Tools: The listening and monitoring platform you use to collect, filter, and analyze the data.
  • Metrics: The numbers you report on and benchmark over time.
  • Cadence and reporting: How often you review data and who receives which insights.

What is a sentiment analysis tool?

A sentiment analysis tool is software that helps you collect and analyze the emotion behind how people talk about your brand online.

Instead of counting the number of mentions or comments, these tools analyze language, tone, and context to understand how people actually feel. Options range from standalone NLP platforms to sentiment features built into social media management suites, and they get used by marketing, PR, customer experience, and product teams alike.

Most sentiment analysis tools use AI and natural language processing (NLP) to do this at scale, making it possible to track sentiment across thousands of conversations in real time.

How does sentiment analysis work?

Sentiment analysis tools use AI, machine learning, and natural language processing to find social mentions of your brand or products on dozens (or hundreds) of websites and apps. Then, they calculate a sentiment score in seconds.

At a high level, social media sentiment analysis follows a four-step process:

  1. Data collection: First, the tool gathers mentions of your brand, products, or keywords from social media platforms, online reviews, forums, and blogs.
  2. Analyze language with AI and NLP: Next, AI models dig into the data itself. They look at context, phrasing, emojis, and the tone of each mention.
  3. Classify sentiment: Each mention gets labeled as positive, negative, or neutral. Many tools also add a sentiment score to show how strongly someone feels, whether it’s mild praise or full-on frustration.
  4. Turn data into insights: Finally, the tool pulls everything together. You can spot trends, recurring themes, influential voices, and how sentiment changes over time.

Not every tool gets to that score the same way. Older platforms lean on rule-based methods that match words against a predefined list of positive and negative terms.

Most modern tools use machine learning models trained on huge volumes of labeled text, and a growing number layer generative AI on top to summarize themes in plain language. This is part of an AI models and platforms market projected to reach $64 billion in 2026. Hybrid approaches combine rules for known edge cases with models for everything else.

One of the biggest advantages of sentiment analysis is seeing changes as they happen. Is your PR campaign lifting customer opinions of your brand? Did the latest recall leave your audience with a bad taste in their mouth? A sentiment analysis tool will tell you. The type of analysis you run shapes how much detail you get, which is what we’ll look at next.

What are the different types of sentiment analysis?

There are four main types of sentiment analysis, and each one answers a slightly different question. Knowing which type you need makes it much easier to shortlist tools, because not every platform supports all four.

Fine-grained sentiment analysis

Fine-grained analysis scores mentions on a scale rather than sorting them into three buckets. Instead of just “negative,” you’ll see the difference between mild disappointment and genuine anger. It’s useful when you need to track small shifts over time or map social sentiment against survey-style scores.

Aspect-based sentiment analysis

Aspect-based sentiment analysis breaks a single mention into the attributes it touches on: price, quality, shipping, support, and so on. That matters because one post can be positive about your product and negative about your delivery times. Product and customer experience teams get the most value here, since the output points directly at what to fix.

Emotion detection

Emotion detection goes past polarity to identify what people are actually feeling, like joy, anger, fear, or surprise. Several tools on this list include it, including Brand24, Meltwater, and Buffer. It’s especially handy during launches and crises, when a shift from surprise to anger tells you more than a dip in your overall score.

Intent-based sentiment analysis

Intent-based analysis looks at what the person wants next. A mention might signal purchase intent, a complaint, a question, or a recommendation, and each one belongs in a different queue. Teams use this to route conversations to sales or support instead of treating every mention as a marketing signal.

When it comes to SEO, forecasting can be a tricky concept.

You’re trying to predict the future of your website’s traffic and it can be difficult to know which metrics to focus on. It can also be difficult to know if the metrics you selected are giving you and your team a clear picture.

That picture has gotten harder to read. AI Overviews, zero-click behavior, and LLM-referred traffic have changed what SEO forecasts need to measure and how the results need to be presented. 

This is why many SEO forecasts are starting to break down. Rankings may improve while clicks flatten. Traffic may increase without revenue following. And visibility may influence demand long before a user ever lands on your site. Modern SEO forecasting needs to explain that disconnect, not hide it.

In this article, we’ll discuss what SEO forecasting is, and where it is and isn’t effective. We’ll also look at the different types of forecasting you can use, as well as the pros and cons of each method. Finally, we’ll cover some of the overall limitations of SEO forecasting as a concept, and what you may want to consider instead.

Let’s start by discussing the potential value of SEO forecasting in the first place.

What Is SEO Forecasting and Why Does It Matter?

SEO forecasting is the practice of predicting and estimating changes in your website’s search engine visibility. This includes factors such as organic traffic, keyword rankings, and more. By trying to predict the future, you can plan ahead and make educated decisions about how to best optimize your website for search engine results pages (SERPs).

For example, let’s say you noticed that your website is losing traffic due to changes in the SERPs. In this case, you may try to use SEO forecasting to help you identify potential issues and strategize how to improve your website’s visibility.

Knowing where your website stands in terms of SEO today is important, but understanding where it’s going in the future is even more critical. With SEO forecasting, in theory, you can identify potential problems and take action to address them before they become a reality. This could include creating content around specific topics or introducing new strategies like link building.

Source: Simplilearn

When used in the right context, SEO forecasting can help give you an idea of performance over time, so you can track progress and adjust as needed. It may also help you stay ahead of the competition and ensure your website is always optimized for success.

With that said, whenever someone asks my NP Digital team about forecasting, we always try to provide a clear picture of what forecasting can and can’t do.

An SEO forecast isn’t going to magically predict the entire future landscape for you. There are too many factors to consider, from seasonality to greater economic trends, that can affect your organic growth and won’t get tracked in any forecast.

So when we talk about SEO forecasting and its benefits, they are best served to help you make decisions, not be your sole source of truth. In addition, if you decide to use them, that needs to be done alongside general best practices like experience, expertise, authoritativeness, and trustworthiness (E-E-A-T), as well as your previous successes or struggles.

Remember, you can’t truly pinpoint search performance until after the fact, which applies to just about any marketing context, really.

The search landscape has also changed materially since most forecasting frameworks were built. AI Overviews, zero-click behavior, and LLM-referred traffic all affect how rankings translate to traffic and how traffic translates to revenue. A forecast that doesn’t account for these shifts will consistently overstate expected results.

A model that treats session volume as a reliable conversion proxy will overstate business outcomes.

Conversion rates are often held constant, yet they shift with buyer intent, market conditions, and the competitive landscape. A model that holds conversion rate constant across changing conditions will produce projections that drift from reality the longer the forecast runs.

Key Takeaways

  • A Peec AI study of 5 million query fanouts collected between April 1 and April 21, 2026 reveals how AI platforms rewrite and expand user queries before executing searches.

Most marketers optimizing for AI search visibility are focused on the wrong layer. They are tracking citations, which is the output. What they should be studying is fanouts, which is the input that determines whether a citation is even possible.

A new analysis of five million query fanouts from ChatGPT, Perplexity, and Grok reveals how AI search platforms actually work behind the scenes, and what that means for how brands show up in AI-generated answers.

How Query Fanouts Actually Work

When a user asks ChatGPT a question, the model does not simply search for that exact phrase. It executes a set of related sub-queries behind the scenes, each exploring a different angle of the original prompt, then merges those results to build its response. That set of sub-queries is the fanout.

A question like “best project management tools for remote teams” might produce fanouts for “top project management software 2026,” “remote team collaboration features,” “project management pricing comparison,” and “enterprise versus small team project management tools,” all running simultaneously. The answer ChatGPT provides draws from all of those sources combined, not just from content that matches the original wording.

Source

ChatGPT uses Reciprocal Rank Fusion to combine scores across these sub-queries. This means content that appears across multiple fanout searches is weighted more heavily than content that only surfaces for one. Covering a topic thoroughly from multiple angles increases your citation probability because content surfacing across more sub-queries scores higher under RRF.

What the Reddit Signal Actually Means

The most actionable finding from the fanout data is the rise of Reddit as a deliberate source. ChatGPT’s query fanouts explicitly referencing Reddit grew from approximately 0.15 percent to 3.68 percent between January and May 2026. This is not incidental. It reflects a pattern where AI systems seek out human-centered, experiential content that branded or editorial sources often do not provide.

Reddit provides something that polished brand content typically cannot: unfiltered customer sentiment, specific use-case discussions, and genuine peer-to-peer evaluations of products and services. AI systems appear to be recognizing that value explicitly, surfacing Reddit as a source for the kind of human validation that helps construct credible answers.

For brands, this creates two implications. First, your presence and reputation within relevant Reddit communities now directly influences what AI systems say about you. Second, the broader principle is that AI platforms are seeking out authentic experiential content as a distinct source type from authoritative or editorial content. Both matter, and they are sourced differently.

Fanouts Before Citations: The Right Audit Sequence

Most AEO work currently focuses on citation tracking: which AI platforms mention your brand, in what context, and with what sentiment. Citation tracking is valuable, but it is a lagging indicator. By the time a citation appears or fails to appear, the fanout decisions that determined it have already been made.

Fanout analysis is the leading indicator. It reveals which angles, source types, and content formats AI systems are actively looking for when a user asks a question in your category. Knowing that ChatGPT consistently injects “best,” “reviews,” and the current year into queries means you can build content that specifically addresses those retrieval patterns, beyond the surface-level keywords your audience uses.

The practical audit sequence should run from fanout to source type to citation. Start by identifying the fanout patterns for the high-intent queries in your category. Then assess which source types are being pulled for each fanout. Then determine where your content appears or fails to appear across those source types. The gap between where your content exists and where AI systems are looking is the optimization target.

articles.title: Google Search Is Becoming AI Search: What This Means for Your Brand
articles.fullContent:
Key Takeaways

  • Google’s AI Mode has surpassed one billion monthly users in its first year, with queries more than doubling every quarter.
  • The new Intelligent Search Box accepts text, images, files, videos, and Chrome tabs as inputs, powered by Gemini 3.5 Flash.
  • Information Agents run 24/7 in the background, monitoring the web on the behalf of users without requiring active searches.
  • Agentic Search allows users to build custom tools, dashboards, and trackers directly inside Search.
  • Brands that are already investing in structured, authoritative, intent-led content are best positioned for this shift.
  • Click-through rates for position one rankings have already collapsed from 27 percent to 11 percent, meaning rankings have never mattered more.

Is Google Search still “search” at all? At Google I/O 2026, Search VP Liz Reid said it plainly: “Google search is AI search.” That’s not a product update. That’s a declaration that the platform has fundamentally changed what it is and what it does.

For marketers, the implications are significant. However, they’re not as disruptive as the headlines suggest, provided you’ve already been doing the work that matters.

What Google Actually Announced

The I/O 2026 announcements covered three distinct capabilities rolling out across Google Search.

The first is the Intelligent Search Box, described by Liz Reid as the biggest upgrade to the search interface in over 25 years. The redesigned input field dynamically expands for complex queries, accepts multiple input types including files, images, and open Chrome tabs. It also replaces traditional autocomplete with AI-powered intent suggestions. AI Overviews and AI Mode are now unified inside a single interface.

The second is Information Agents, persistent background systems that monitor the web 24 hours a day on behalf of users. Rather than requiring a user to return and search again, an information agent continuously tracks changes across blogs, news sites, social posts, and real-time data sources, then sends a synthesized update when something relevant shifts. The practical parallel is Google Alerts, rebuilt with an LLM’s ability to reason about what it finds.

The third is Agentic Search, which allows users to build custom mini-apps, dashboards, and trackers from inside Search using Gemini Spark and Google Antigravity. A query about tracking market movements can produce a live monitoring tool, while questions about apartment hunting can generate a filter and alert system. Search is no longer returning links. It’s producing outputs.

What This Means for Organic Search

The honest read on these announcements is that traditional ranking behavior is already changing. SISTRIX data published in March 2026 documented a collapse in position-one click-through rates in Germany, from 27 percent to 11 percent. AI overviews already reach 2.5 billion monthly users, and AI Mode crossed one billion monthly users in its first year.

Users are already getting answers without clicking, and in the future, Information Agents will provide users with information without initiating a search at all. The interaction model is shifting from reactive to proactive on Google’s end.

For brands, this changes two things. First, appearing in AI-generated answers is now as important as ranking in traditional results. Second, being visible to information agents is a new form of visibility that did not exist before. Both depend on the same foundation: content that is clear, authoritative, structured, and genuinely useful.

Why Existing SEO Foundations Still Win

The temptation after an announcement like this is to treat everything as a disruption requiring new tactics but the reality is more grounding. The structures we have been building (e.g., entity authority, intent-matched content, technical accessibility, and strong E-E-A-T signals) are precisely what AI-native search rewards.
